voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.
title: Gravitation applications: depth, escape and satellites

sources.title: Official NTA JEE Main 2026 syllabus: Unit 6

chapters.title: Gravity, potential and escape
chapters.formula: g_out = GM/r^2; g_inside = g0 r/R; V_out = -GM/r; v_escape = sqrt(2GM/r)
points: Use r = R + h outside; the depth rule assumes uniform density and no rotation.
At h = R, g = g0/4; at depth 3R/4, uniform-sphere g = g0/4.
Field may be zero while potential is negative. Escape uses total energy, not constant-g mgh.
chapters.script: Welcome back. Let's connect gravity on the ground with escape into space. Our planet is spherical, and we ignore rotation. Outside it, gravitational force is G times capital M times little m, divided by radius squared. Divide by the test mass to get gravitational acceleration. Radius means distance from the centre, not height above the ground. At height h, radius is R plus h. Surface gravity is g zero. The gravity ratio is R divided by R plus h, all squared. Try a height equal to the planet's radius. Pause. The centre distance doubles, so gravity becomes one quarter of surface gravity. For height much smaller than R, the ratio is approximately one minus two h over R. Do not use that shortcut at height R. Inside a uniform density planet, outer spherical shells cancel their field. Enclosed mass grows as radius cubed, so gravity grows linearly with radius. At depth d, gravity is g zero times one minus d over R. For one quarter of surface gravity, solve one minus d over R equals one quarter. The depth is three quarters of R. The outside height was R; same gravity, different locations. Real Earth has varying density, so the interior line is an ideal model. Now choose potential zero at infinity. Outside, potential V is minus G M over r. Potential energy is little m times V. Moving outward makes energy less negative: lifting from R to two R requires G M m over two R if initial and final speeds are zero. Constant g times m times h works only for small heights. Field and potential are different. Equal masses on opposite sides cancel their fields at the midpoint, but their negative potentials add. Inside our uniform sphere, potential is minus G M times three R squared minus r squared, divided by two R cubed. At the centre, field is zero but potential is minus three G M over two R. Finally, escape needs just enough energy to reach infinity with zero final speed. One half m v squared minus G M m over r equals zero. Escape speed is the square root of two G M over r, independent of test mass. For a radial surface launch at half escape speed, kinetic energy is G M m over four R. Total energy is minus three G M m over four R. At the highest point, speed is zero. Solving gives radius four R over three, hence height R over three. This assumes no drag or later propulsion. A nonradial orbit retains tangential speed at its turning point, so that last step cannot be copied blindly.

chapters.title: Satellite energy and Kepler's laws
chapters.formula: v_circular = sqrt(GM/r); T = 2pi sqrt(r^3/GM); E_circular = -GMm/(2r); T_ellipse^2 = 4pi^2 a^3/GM
points: Gravity supplies centripetal acceleration; an orbit is free fall, not absence of gravity.
At 4r, circular speed halves, period multiplies by 8 and energy becomes less negative.
An ellipse has the central mass at a focus. Equal areas follow from conserved angular momentum; use semi-major axis a for period and energy.
chapters.script: A satellite keeps falling, yet keeps missing the ground. Gravity changes the direction of its velocity. For a circular orbit, G M m over r squared equals m v squared over r. Cancel mass and one radius: circular speed is the square root of G M over r. Period is circumference divided by speed, giving two pi times the square root of r cubed over G M. Always add the planet's radius to the supplied height. Let's compare equal mass satellites at radii r and four r around the same planet. What happens to speed and period? Pause. Speed halves because it scales as the inverse square root of radius. Period multiplies by eight because it scales as radius to the power three halves. Potential energy is minus G M m over r. Circular kinetic energy is positive G M m over two r, so total energy is negative G M m over two r. In the outer orbit, total energy is minus G M m over eight r. Subtract the inner value: the increase is positive three G M m over eight r. Raising an orbit requires energy even though its circular speed decreases. This difference is not a single burn instruction; actual transfers involve intermediate motion. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft accelerate together. Gravity still acts, but a freely floating astronaut has nearly zero support force. A geostationary satellite needs a circular equatorial orbit in Earth's rotation direction with the sidereal period, approximately eighty six thousand one hundred sixty four seconds. A one day period alone is insufficient. Now extend the picture to an ellipse. Kepler's first law places the attracting body at one focus, not the centre. The second law gives equal swept areas in equal times. Why? Gravity is central, so its torque about the attracting centre is zero. Angular momentum stays constant, and the areal rate is angular momentum divided by twice the orbiting mass. At nearest and farthest points, velocity is perpendicular to radius. Therefore nearest radius times nearest speed equals farthest radius times farthest speed. If the farthest radius is three times the nearest, the nearest speed is three times the farthest speed. Equal areas do not mean equal distances. Kepler's third law says period squared scales as semi major axis cubed for bodies around the same dominant central mass. With nearest radius R and farthest radius three R, the semi major axis is their average, two R. Compared with a circle of radius R, the period is two times the square root of two. Elliptical total energy is minus G M m over twice the semi major axis, giving minus G M m over four R here. Do not replace that axis by the changing instantaneous radius. These are ideal two body results with negligible satellite mass. Use the written lesson for additional steps, then test the radius, energy and model assumptions before trusting an answer.

quiz.question: At height R above a spherical planet of radius R, gravity is:
quiz.explanation: Centre distance is 2R; inverse-square gravity becomes g0/4.

quiz.question: At depth R/2 in an ideal uniform-density planet, gravity is:
quiz.explanation: The interior relation g = g0(1-d/R) gives g0/2; rotation is neglected.

quiz.question: Escape speed divided by circular orbital speed at the same radius is:
quiz.explanation: Divide sqrt(2GM/r) by sqrt(GM/r) to obtain sqrt(2).

quiz.question: Changing circular-orbit radius from r to 4r around the same planet multiplies period by:
quiz.explanation: Period scales as r^(3/2), hence the factor is 4^(3/2) = 8.

quiz.question: A bound ellipse has nearest radius R and farthest radius 3R. Its semi-major axis is:
quiz.explanation: The semi-major axis is half the sum of the nearest and farthest radii: (R+3R)/2 = 2R.
